title: Top incident types analysis — 2025 Q1 (baseline for taxonomy v1)
author: Miles Thornton
body:
## Purpose
This page summarizes production incidents observed in **2025 Q1 (Jan 1–Mar 31, 2025)** and clusters them into a small set of **top incident types**. The goals are to:
- Establish a **baseline** (volume, customer impact, time-to-mitigate / MTTR) before taxonomy v1 rollout.
- Identify the **highest-leverage categories** to prioritize in the initial taxonomy (simple enough for live response).
- Surface repeat contributors (capacity, rollouts, dependency failures) to inform follow-on reliability work.

This is not a postmortem-of-postmortems; it is an aggregate view intended to drive taxonomy/ownership decisions and reporting.

## Data sources
- Incident channel records + incident tool exports (Sev1–Sev3)
- SRE on-call handoff notes and statuspage entries
- Support escalations (Jira) when tied to an incident
- Manual labeling in the incident inventory sheet (see Appendix)

**Included**
- Hosted API incidents (all regions)
- Dedicated pool incidents (all regions)
- Private incidents where Redwood is primary operator (day-2 ops), when present in incident tool

**Excluded**
- Security incidents governed by Security IR process (may share metadata fields later)
- Sev4 / “FYI” events and internal-only disruptions without prod impact

## Definitions
- **Customer-impacting incident:** Customer-visible error rate increase, elevated latency, timeouts/disconnects, or partial unavailability affecting production traffic.
- **TTM (time to mitigate):** time from incident declared to a mitigation in place (even if not fully resolved).
- **MTTR:** time from incident declared to service restored within SLO/expected baseline.
- **Incident types vs contributing factors:** A single incident has **one primary type** for reporting, with 0+ contributing factors.

## Executive summary (Q1 baseline)
### Overall volume and severity
In Q1 we recorded **86 production incidents** (Sev1–Sev3).

| Metric | Value |
|---|---:|
| Total incidents (Sev1–Sev3) | 86 |
| Sev1 | 11 |
| Sev2 | 29 |
| Sev3 | 46 |
| Customer-impacting (any severity) | 61 (71%) |
| Incidents with Support escalation attached | 24 (28%) |

### Deployment surface distribution
| Surface | Incidents | Customer-impacting | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Hosted API | 52 | 41 | Mix of routing/gateway/runtime issues; largest volume driver |
| Dedicated | 28 | 17 | High share of capacity saturation + autoscaling/pool misconfig |
| Private (Redwood-operated) | 6 | 3 | Low volume; higher median time to mitigation due to access/coordination |

### Response-time baseline (all severities)
| Metric | Q1 value |
|---|---:|
| Median TTM | 18 min |
| P90 TTM | 61 min |
| Median MTTR | 64 min |
| P90 MTTR | 4.2 hrs |

**Observation:** A small number of categories account for most long-duration incidents (MTTR P90 tail). These categories are good candidates for explicit taxonomy values and remediation SLA mapping.

## Top incident types (clustered)
We clustered incidents into primary types based on the initial incident writeups and follow-up review. The goal was to minimize ambiguity and keep categories actionable.

### Top 10 incident types by volume (Q1)
| Rank | Primary incident type (cluster label) | Count | % of total | Customer-impacting % | Median MTTR | P90 MTTR |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | Routing/policy misroute or overload (control plane + smart routing) | 16 | 18.6% | 88% | 58 min | 3.6 hrs |
| 2 | Capacity exhaustion (fleet/pool saturation) | 14 | 16.3% | 79% | 71 min | 5.1 hrs |
| 3 | Gateway/edge streaming & connection handling | 9 | 10.5% | 100% | 49 min | 2.4 hrs |
| 4 | Runtime crash / OOM / kernel fault | 8 | 9.3% | 75% | 83 min | 6.0 hrs |
| 5 | Autoscaling policy/regression (scale triggers, warmup, headroom) | 7 | 8.1% | 57% | 96 min | 4.7 hrs |
| 6 | Upstream provider/network degradation (cloud region, LB, DNS) | 6 | 7.0% | 83% | 44 min | 2.2 hrs |
| 7 | Model-specific instability (bad weights, quant profile mismatch, tokenizer edge cases) | 6 | 7.0% | 67% | 102 min | 6.5 hrs |
| 8 | Quotas/rate limiting/auth misconfiguration | 5 | 5.8% | 60% | 31 min | 1.1 hrs |
| 9 | Observability/telemetry pipeline breaks (blindness during incidents) | 5 | 5.8% | 20% | 78 min | 3.9 hrs |
| 10 | Release/config rollout error (feature flag, config schema, bad default) | 4 | 4.7% | 75% | 67 min | 3.0 hrs |

**Coverage:** These 10 types account for **80/86 incidents (93%)**. The remaining 6 were “one-off” types (e.g., internal admin tooling outage, isolated billing/usage reporting delay).

## Customer impact profile
### Impact symptoms observed (customer-visible)
Across the 61 customer-impacting incidents, the most common symptoms were:
- Elevated **5xx / upstream errors** (especially from routing overload or runtime crash loops)
- **Tail latency** regressions (P95/P99) without full outage (often capacity headroom + batching dynamics)
- **Streaming disconnects** or partial response truncation (edge/gateway)
- **Increased 429/403** due to quota/rate-limit config mismatches (less frequent but high support friction)

### Customer tier notes
- **Dedicated incidents** were fewer in count but disproportionately represented in **enterprise escalations** and **formal comms** (named accounts, contractual context).
- Hosted incidents tended to affect more customers but with faster mitigations via routing changes/fallbacks.

## Where time was spent (qualitative)
We reviewed timelines for the 20 longest MTTR incidents. Repeating sources of delay:
1) **Ambiguous ownership at declare time** (routing vs fleet vs runtime), leading to multi-team paging.
2) **Slow detection of blast radius** (missing “impacted surface” + region tagging; dashboards not aligned to incident types).
3) **Mitigation requires capacity movement** (rebalancing pools, provisioning, or rollback windows).
4) **Model-specific failures** requiring SME involvement (runtime + model onboarding), with longer diagnosis loops.

These are directly addressable via taxonomy fields + ownership mapping + response SLAs.

## Detailed type notes (definition + example patterns)
This section provides working definitions we used while clustering. These definitions informed taxonomy v1 proposals.

### 1) Routing/policy misroute or overload
**What it looks like:**
- Sudden shift of traffic to a subset of pools/regions
- Fallback policies not engaging (or engaging too broadly)
- Elevated 5xx/timeouts concentrated by route or model

**Common triggers (contributing factors):**
- New routing policy rollout
- Inconsistent capacity signals feeding router
- Control plane config propagation delay

**Why it matters:** Highest volume category and a major driver of Sev1.

### 2) Capacity exhaustion (fleet/pool saturation)
**What it looks like:**
- GPU pools at/near 100% utilization
- Queue growth; tail latency climbs then timeouts
- Dedicated pools: predictable saturation during customer batch jobs

**Common triggers:**
- Under-provisioning vs demand
- Provisioning lag or GPU scarcity
- Headroom misconfiguration

**Why it matters:** Second-highest volume and long MTTR tail when provisioning is required.

### 3) Gateway/edge streaming & connection handling
**What it looks like:**
- Streaming disconnect spikes
- Partial responses; client retries amplify load
- Concentrated at specific edge POPs or gateway versions

**Common triggers:**
- Gateway release
- Connection idle timeout changes
- LB behavior changes upstream

**Why it matters:** 100% customer-visible and high support ticket volume per incident.

### 4) Runtime crash / OOM / kernel fault
**What it looks like:**
- Crash loops on inference workers
- OOM under specific prompt/sequence distributions
- Kernel faults tied to specific GPU types/driver combinations

**Common triggers:**
- Runtime build/regression
- New model deployment / quantization profile mismatch
- Batching/caching tuning changes

**Why it matters:** Lower volume but disproportionately contributes to Sev1 and long MTTR when diagnosis is complex.

### 5) Autoscaling policy/regression
**What it looks like:**
- Scale-out not triggering or triggering late
- Warmup times not accounted for
- Scale-in too aggressive causing oscillation

**Common triggers:**
- Policy changes without load test
- Metrics lag or incorrect signal selection

**Why it matters:** Often misclassified as “capacity”; taxonomy needs a clear boundary to route ownership correctly.

## Recommended taxonomy v1 priorities (based on Q1)
To keep taxonomy usable during live response, we recommend taxonomy v1 emphasize the categories that:
- occur frequently,
- drive meaningful customer impact, and/or
- create ownership ambiguity.

**Priority categories for v1 (must be first-class values):**
1) Routing / control plane degradation
2) Capacity exhaustion (fleet/pool)
3) Autoscaling policy failure
4) Gateway/edge streaming
5) Runtime crash / worker instability
6) Model-specific instability
7) Upstream provider/network degradation
8) Auth/quota/rate-limit misconfiguration

**Why these:** They cover the majority of incidents and align with clear remediation playbooks and owning teams (Platform, Infra/Fleet, Runtime, Networking).

## Baseline metrics to track after taxonomy rollout
To measure whether taxonomy + ownership mapping improves outcomes, we will track (monthly):
- **% incidents with category+owner set within 15 minutes** of declaration
- **Median TTM and MTTR** by primary category (and by owner team)
- **Reclassification rate** (declare-time category changed post-incident) as a signal of ambiguous definitions
- **Top contributing factors** (release, capacity planning, dependency, config) tied to categories
- **Support friction indicators**: number of support escalations per incident and time to first engineering response

## Limitations / caveats
- Clustering was done from incident writeups and available Slack timelines; some incidents lacked complete data.
- A few incidents could reasonably map to multiple types (e.g., routing overload caused by capacity scarcity). We assigned a single primary type to avoid double-counting; contributing factors should capture the remainder.
- Private (Redwood-operated) volume is low; Q1 results may not generalize.

## Appendix A: Links / artifacts
- Incident inventory and clustering sheet: sources/google_drive/shared_drives/engineering/site-reliability-engineering/incident-inventory-and-clustering-sheet.json
- Ownership map (service/team): sources/google_drive/shared_drives/engineering/platform-engineering/ownership-map-services-sheet.json
- Example Support tickets used during clustering:
  - SUP-1842 (recurring 5xx/timeouts; ownership ambiguity)
  - SUP-1910 (Dedicated saturation; capacity/autoscaling boundary)
  - SUP-1977 (streaming disconnects; edge vs runtime)

## Appendix B: Raw counts by severity (top types)
| Type | Sev1 | Sev2 | Sev3 | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Routing/policy misroute or overload | 4 | 7 | 5 | 16 |
| Capacity exhaustion (fleet/pool saturation) | 2 | 5 | 7 | 14 |
| Gateway/edge streaming | 2 | 4 | 3 | 9 |
| Runtime crash / OOM / kernel fault | 2 | 2 | 4 | 8 |
| Autoscaling policy/regression | 0 | 3 | 4 | 7 |
| Upstream provider/network degradation | 1 | 3 | 2 | 6 |
| Model-specific instability | 0 | 3 | 3 | 6 |
| Quotas/rate limiting/auth misconfiguration | 0 | 2 | 3 | 5 |
| Observability/telemetry pipeline breaks | 0 | 0 | 5 | 5 |
| Release/config rollout error | 0 | 0 | 4 | 4 |

## Appendix C: Actionable takeaways for taxonomy v1 doc
These points should be reflected explicitly in the taxonomy guidance:
- Provide a short “decision tree” for **capacity vs autoscaling vs routing overload**.
- For “Gateway/edge streaming”, require capturing **client symptom** (disconnect vs truncation vs latency) and **edge POP/region**.
- For runtime/model issues, strongly encourage recording **model id + version + quant profile** at declare time.
- Add an explicit “Upstream provider/network” type to prevent these incidents defaulting to “unknown” and obscuring trends.

(End of Q1 baseline.)
